newsitem.title: FINLAND: INTERVIEW - FOREX RATES NO PROBLEM TO FINLAND BANK.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - FOREX RATES NO PROBLEM TO FINLAND BANK.

text.p: The markka's current deviation from the central parity rate in the ERM -- 3.04 against the German mark -- is modest and exchange rates no problem, Bank of Finland board member Matti Vanhala said on Thursday.
In an interview with Reuters, he said the central bank had been intervening and would continue to on the market to cap fluctuation, but saw no trend in recent markka movements.
"We are somehwere between two and three percent from the central rate, but it's a modest deviation really," he said.

"I'm not sure what we would do if there was a trend, but there has not been any trend. There has been a modest persistent interest to increase markka holdings but we are not talking about (such) huge sums it would be a trend," he said.
Asked whether current exchange rates were a problem for the central bank, he said "no". "We have been remarkably steady."
DEM/FIM was 2.9500 at Wednesday's interbank market close, some three percent stronger than the markka's key 3.04 DEM/FIM parity rate in Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism.
Vanhala repeated that the central bank had no hidden band for the markka's fluctuations and noted that the official bands in the ERM are 15 percent either way.

"What we want to see is calm stable conditions in the market and that is why we go from time to time into the market to steady the movement," he said. "We have done that from time to time and we will be doing that from time to time in the future."
But these actions should not be considered "monetary policy proper", he said.
A very rough analysis suggests equilibrium exchange rates are broadly around the ERM central parity rates, he said.
"From that point of view, the current level in the markka, around 2.5 percent or wherever it is off the central rate, it is in the same ballpark," he said.

Vanhala said Finland's economic situation had not changed from mid-June. Then the central bank said the risks had increased of inflation rising above tolerable levels around two percent, warning that if they increased more, it would force the Bank to consider monetary tightening.
"We don't feel that we deliberately now need to tighten or loosen, we are happy with the current stance," he said.

Vanhala said inflation would normalise -- the Bank forecasts core inflation rising to slightly above two percent next year with the consumer price index rising more -- although it was also possible that behaviour has become less inflationary.
"It is possible that the inflation mechanism in Finland has changed ... that there could be sustained strong growth and moderate inflation," he said.

"We want to give a chance to the hypothesis that inflation behaviour has changed," he said, adding that this was being tested all the time, and would be tested in coming collective pay talks for 1998 in the autumn.

The last time the Bank of Finland raised its key tender rate was in 1995, just as the collective wage-bargaining season was getting under way. It then made a series of cuts and the rate now matches Germany's 3.00 percent repo.
So far, Vanhala said the tone in labour market rhetoric ahead of the pay talks "has actually been quite moderate".
However, he added it was reasonable for market operators to anticipate inflation, in Finland among the lowest levels in Europe at 0.2 percent in June, would rise to normal levels.
This already shows in markka yields. September forward rates have risen some 11 basis points to around 3.32 percent since the central bank's June comments on inflation.
"Probably there is a sort of expectation in the yield curve, some sort of expectation that perhaps the bank will at some stage raise the interest rate," he said.
Asked whether this was reasonable, he said: "Yes, why not, but it depends on what they have for inflation expectations themselves."
But he said he could not say whether markka strength could delay a rate hike, or compensate for one as a stronger currency means tighter monetary conditions.
Commentators have said the central bank is in a tough position, citing an appreciating trend in the markka against a possible need to raise interest rates.
